style: Say curiously and warmly, like a friendly school librarian talking to young children
lines: How many legs does a spider have?
A book about spiders will tell us: eight!
Will a plant grow faster by the window or in the closet?
Grow two plants and watch them for two weeks.
What does a firefighter do all day?
Invite a firefighter to visit, or write them a letter.
Does a heavy ball roll down a ramp faster than a light ball?
Build a ramp and race them!
Where do penguins live?
A nonfiction book or a map can show us.
How do you take care of a sick dog?
A veterinarian knows best. A pet care book helps too.
Which paper towel soaks up the most water?
Test three kinds with the same amount of water.
What was our school like 50 years ago?
Ask someone who went here long ago, or look at old yearbooks.
What do sharks eat?
An ocean animal book will tell us.
Does ice melt faster in the sun or in the shade?
Put two ice cubes out and time them.
How does a dentist fix a cavity?
A dentist can explain it at your next visit.
How tall is the tallest tree in the world?
Scientists measured it, and books share it. It's taller than a 30-story building!
What makes a good bread recipe?
Ask a baker, then try baking it yourself.
Will a magnet pick up a paper clip? A penny? A spoon?
Grab a magnet and test each one.
Why do leaves change color in fall?
A science book explains it, or ask a park ranger.
How do you build a bridge that won't fall down?
An engineer can tell us, and we can build one with blocks.
What do astronauts eat in space?
Space books and NASA have pictures. Some classes even talk with astronauts!
Which way does a shadow point in the morning?
Go outside in the morning and look.
How could we find out?
Look it up!

Who...
What...
Where...
When...
Why...
How...
Which question helps us learn more?
or
Do frogs eat?
What do frogs eat, and how do they catch it?
A yes-or-no question stops at "yes." The second one makes us learn something new.
Why is the sky blue?
Is the sky blue?
"Why" questions dig deeper. We can already see that the sky is blue!
Are volcanoes hot?
What happens inside a volcano before it erupts?
The second question has a lot to discover. The first one is answered in one word.
How do bees make honey?
Do bees like flowers?
"How" questions lead to steps and details.
Is the ocean big?
What lives at the very bottom of the ocean?
The second question takes us somewhere new.
How did people talk to each other before phones?
Did people have phones long ago?
"How did people..." opens up stories about letters, messengers and more.
Is my dog smart?
How do dogs learn new tricks?
The second question can be answered by looking it up or asking a dog trainer.
Yes!
Look at the other one.
